title: A request for a cassette's bare address counts as a miss, so a health probe from outside fails a replay that served every recorded call
foundBy: session agent replaying a multi-member campaign through cs-vcr, several replays at a time on one shared host

evidence.verified: go test ./internal/proxy/ -run "TestAProbe|TestAPostToTheBareAddress" -count=20 and go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestAProbeDoesNotFailAReplay -count=20: PASS. Before the fix the replay test answered 400 cassette_miss and the record test logged `the probe reached the provider` with 2 entries. Against bin/cs-vcr on the committed cassettes, two curl probes gave 200, and the summary read `misses 0`, `probes 2`, exit status 0.

resolution: cs-vcr answers a bodiless request for a bare cassette address itself, in both kinds of session, before selection and before forwarding. It counts a probe and nothing else.
details:
**What happened.** A campaign of several agents was replayed through `cs-vcr replay`. Each agent's base address was the proxy's address for its own cassette, of the form `/c/<provider>/<cassette>`. Somebody on the host ran `cs-sandbox doctor`, which checks that each credential lender reaches its upstream by asking for that bare address. For each agent that was up, the proxy logged a `cassette miss` with `target=/` and the reason `this run asked for / instead`. The summary then showed `misses` and `rejected` equal to the number of probes, and `requests` larger than `replayed` by the same number. The process then gave exit status 4. Every recorded call had been served, in order.

**Why it matters.** A miss means that the client asked something the recording does not hold. This request did not come from the client, and it is not a call to any provider surface. The probe does not move the cassette's position, which is right, so the only harm is the count and the exit status. A person who looks at the machine while a replay runs fails it. A consumer can work around this by subtracting the misses whose target is `/`, and that is a rule each consumer has to discover. SBX-048 asks for the probe to change on its side.

**What is asked for.** Answer a request for `/` under a known cassette without counting a miss, and count it apart, as `probes` for example. Rule R6 already serves a client's repeated `GET /models` probe again, and VCR-023 settled how a late one is placed. This is the same idea for a request that matches no provider route at all.

**The record mode twin is not tested.** `serve_command.go` says that anything unrecognised on the proxied port is forwarded to a provider. A probe that arrives during `cs-vcr record` may therefore reach the provider, or be written into the cassette as a step that no replay will ever make. Somebody should check that before a recording made on a shared host is trusted.

**How to reproduce.** Start `cs-vcr replay --cassettes DIR`, run `curl http://127.0.0.1:PORT/c/<provider>/<cassette>`, and stop the proxy. The summary shows `misses 1` and the exit status is 4.

notes.text: The record mode twin is real. A test written before the fix showed the probe reaching the provider, and the cassette gaining `GET /` as step 1. `record` now answers the probe itself, and does not open the cassette to do it, so a probe cannot create one.

What shipped, for the filer. `GET` or `HEAD` on the bare address answers 200 with `{"cassette","mode","source"}`, and is counted on a `probes` summary line that is left out of `requests`. The fix has two limits that the record did not ask for. A probe of a cassette that `replay` does not hold still answers 404 `unknown_cassette`, so a checker finds a mistyped name. A `POST` to the bare address is still a miss, because that is a client whose base URL lost its path. SPEC rule R21 holds the contract.
